## How authentication is determined¶ {#how-authentication-is-determined}

The authentication schemes are always defined as a list of classes.  REST framework will attempt to authenticate with each class in the list, and will set
`request.user`
and
`request.auth`
using the return value of the first class that successfully authenticates.

If no class authenticates,
`request.user`
will be set to an instance of
`django.contrib.auth.models.AnonymousUser`
, and
`request.auth`
will be set to
`None`
.

The value of
`request.user`
and
`request.auth`
for unauthenticated requests can be modified using the
`UNAUTHENTICATED_USER`
and
`UNAUTHENTICATED_TOKEN`
settings.

## Setting the authentication scheme¶ {#setting-the-authentication-scheme}

The default authentication schemes may be set globally, using the
`DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES`
setting.  For example.

`# Request will only authenticate if `SessionAuthentication` is in use.request=factory.get('/accounts/django-superstars/')request.user=user
response=view(request)`

reference: Set them globally with DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES in your REST_FRAMEWORK settings dict; every view uses that default unless it overrides it per-view or per-viewset.
reference_contexts: The default authentication schemes may be set globally, using the DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES setting.

llm_response:
To enforce authentication for every endpoint at once in Django REST Framework, you should use the global settings `DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES` and `DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES`.

DRF views are opted-out of Django's `LoginRequiredMiddleware` because DRF authentication and permissions are determined after middleware is applied, and because the middleware's redirect behavior is not suitable for APIs, which should return a 401 status code instead.

To set these globally, update your project's settings:

```python
REST_FRAMEWORK = {
    'DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES': [
        # Add your desired authentication classes here
    ],
    'DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES': [
        'rest_framework.permissions.IsAuthenticated',
    ]
}
```

Using `IsAuthenticated` in `DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES` will ensure that all API requests are required to be logged in.

## Django 5.1+LoginRequiredMiddleware¶ {#django-51-loginrequiredmiddleware}

If you're running Django 5.1+ and use the
LoginRequiredMiddleware (https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/ref/middleware/#django.contrib.auth.middleware.LoginRequiredMiddleware)
, please note that all views from DRF are opted-out of this middleware.  This is because the authentication in DRF is based on authentication and permissions classes, which may be determined after the middleware has been applied.  Additionally, when the request is not authenticated, the middleware redirects the user to the login page, which is not suitable for API requests, where it's preferable to return a 401 status code.

REST framework offers an equivalent mechanism for DRF views via the global settings,
`DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES`
and
`DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES`
.  They should be changed accordingly if you need to enforce that API requests are logged in.

`WWW-Authenticate:Basicrealm="api"`

If you use
`BasicAuthentication`
in production you must ensure that your API is only available over
`https`
.  You should also ensure that your API clients will always re-request the username and password at login, and will never store those details to persistent storage.

## API Reference¶ {#api-reference}

### AllowAny¶ {#allowany}

The
`AllowAny`
permission class will allow unrestricted access,
regardless of if the request was authenticated or unauthenticated
.

This permission is not strictly required, since you can achieve the same result by using an empty list or tuple for the permissions setting, but you may find it useful to specify this class because it makes the intention explicit.

### IsAuthenticated¶ {#isauthenticated}

The
`IsAuthenticated`
permission class will deny permission to any unauthenticated user, and allow permission otherwise.

This permission is suitable if you want your API to only be accessible to registered users.

### IsAdminUser¶ {#isadminuser}

The
`IsAdminUser`
permission class will deny permission to any user, unless
`user.is_staff`
is
`True`
in which case permission will be allowed.

This permission is suitable if you want your API to only be accessible to a subset of trusted administrators.

This permission is suitable if you want your API to only be accessible to a subset of trusted administrators.

### IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly¶ {#isauthenticatedorreadonly}

The
`IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly`
will allow authenticated users to perform any request.  Requests for unauthenticated users will only be permitted if the request method is one of the "safe" methods;
`GET`
,
`HEAD`
or
`OPTIONS`
.

This permission is suitable if you want to your API to allow read permissions to anonymous users, and only allow write permissions to authenticated users.

### DjangoModelPermissions¶ {#djangomodelpermissions}

Permission checks are always run at the very start of the view, before any other code is allowed to proceed.  Permission checks will typically use the authentication information in the
`request.user`
and
`request.auth`
properties to determine if the incoming request should be permitted.

Permissions are used to grant or deny access for different classes of users to different parts of the API.

The simplest style of permission would be to allow access to any authenticated user, and deny access to any unauthenticated user. This corresponds to the
`IsAuthenticated`
class in REST framework.

A slightly less strict style of permission would be to allow full access to authenticated users, but allow read-only access to unauthenticated users. This corresponds to the
`IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly`
class in REST framework.

The difference between `AllowAny` and `IsAuthenticated` is as follows:

*   **`AllowAny`**: Allows unrestricted access to the API, regardless of whether the request is authenticated or unauthenticated. user_input: Once a list endpoint is paginated, what does the response body actually look like — how is a client supposed to know how many records exist in total and where to get the next batch?
reference: The results get wrapped in an envelope rather than returned as a bare array. A page-number paginated response carries `count` (the total number of records across all pages), `next` and `previous` (full URLs to the adjacent pages, or null at either end), and `results` (the records for this page). Clients walk the collection by following `next` until it comes back null, rather than by computing page numbers themselves.
reference_contexts: HTTP 200 OK { "count": 1023, "next": "https://api.example.org/accounts/?page=5", "previous": "https://api.example.org/accounts/?page=3", "results": [ ... ] }
llm_response:
The structure of a paginated response depends on the pagination class being used:

**1. Response Body Pagination (e.g., `LimitOffsetPagination` or custom `PageNumberPagination`)**
When using styles like `LimitOffsetPagination` or a custom class that includes pagination in the response body, the JSON response contains the following keys:
*   **`count`**: The total number of records available.
*   **`next`**: A fully-qualified URL to the next batch of records.
*   **`previous`**: A fully-qualified URL to the previous batch of records.
*   **`results`**: The list of records for the current page.

Example structure:
```json
{
    "count": 1023,
    "next": "https://api.example.org/accounts/?limit=100&offset=500",
    "previous": "https://api.example.org/accounts/?limit=100&offset=300",
    "results": [...]
}
```

**2. Header-based Pagination (`LinkHeaderPagination`)**
If `LinkHeaderPagination` is configured, the pagination information is not included in the response body. Instead, the client must look at the **`Link`** header of the HTTP response to determine how to navigate the records.

llm_response:
To enable clients to search your list endpoint using `?search=`, you must perform the following steps:

1.  **Add the filter backend:** Include `filters.SearchFilter` in the `filter_backends` attribute of your view.
2.  **Define search fields:** Set the `search_fields` attribute on your view to a list of the model's text fields (e.g., `CharField` or `TextField`) that you want to be searchable.

Example configuration:

```python
from rest_framework import filters, generics

class UserListView(generics.ListAPIView):
    queryset = User.objects.all()
    serializer_class = UserSerializer
    filter_backends = [filters.SearchFilter]
    search_fields = ['username', 'email']
```

The default query parameter name is `search`. If you need to change this name, you can modify the `SEARCH_PARAM` setting.

llm_response:
To restrict which fields clients can use to order list results, you should explicitly specify the allowed fields by setting an `ordering_fields` attribute on your view. This is the recommended approach to prevent unexpected data leakage.

You can implement this by adding `filters.OrderingFilter` to the `filter_backends` and defining the `ordering_fields` list in your view class:

```python
class UserListView(generics.ListAPIView):
    queryset = User.objects.all()
    serializer_class = UserSerializer
    filter_backends = [filters.OrderingFilter]
    ordering_fields = ['username', 'email']
```

If you do not specify `ordering_fields`, the filter will default to allowing ordering on any readable fields on the serializer. You should avoid using the special value `'__all__'` unless you are confident the queryset contains no sensitive data.

## ModelSerializer API¶ {#modelserializer-api}

The serializer redesign in 3.0 did not include any public API for modifying how ModelSerializer classes automatically generate a set of fields from a given mode class. We've now re-introduced an API for this, allowing you to create new ModelSerializer base classes that behave differently, such as using a different default style for relationships.

user_input: What does serializer.is_valid(raise_exception=True) do?
reference: It raises a serializers.ValidationError on invalid data, which DRF's default exception handler turns into a 400 response automatically.
reference_contexts: The .is_valid() method takes an optional raise_exception flag that will cause it to raise a serializers.ValidationError exception if there are validation errors.
llm_response:
Calling `serializer.is_valid(raise_exception=True)` causes a `serializers.ValidationError` exception to be raised if the serializer data contains validation errors.

This has the following effects:
* **Automatic Error Handling:** The exception is automatically handled by the REST framework's default exception handler, which returns an `HTTP 400 Bad Request` response by default. This allows you to remove manual error response handling from your view code.
* **Global Customization:** You can alter the handling and formatting of these error responses globally by using the `EXCEPTION_HANDLER` setting or by providing a custom exception handler.
* **Generic Views:** This flag is used by generic views, allowing you to override the style of validation error responses globally for your API.

### Validation¶ {#validation}

When deserializing data, you always need to call
`is_valid()`
before attempting to access the validated data, or save an object instance. If any validation errors occur, the
`.errors`
property will contain a dictionary representing the resulting error messages.  For example:


`serializer=CommentSerializer(data={'email':'foobar','content':'baz'})serializer.is_valid()# Falseserializer.errors# {'email': ['Enter a valid email address.'], 'created': ['This field is required.']}`


Each key in the dictionary will be the field name, and the values will be lists of strings of any error messages corresponding to that field.  The
`non_field_errors`
key may also be present, and will list any general validation errors. The name of the
`non_field_errors`
key may be customized using the
`NON_FIELD_ERRORS_KEY`
REST framework setting.

Calling

user_input: Where do I put validation for a single serializer field?

You can perform validation for a single serializer field using the following approaches:

*   **`validate_<field_name>` method:** You can add a method named `.validate_<field_name>` to your `Serializer` subclass. Note that if the field is declared with `required=False`, this validation step will not occur if the field is not included in the data.

#### Change tovalidate_<field_name>.¶ {#change-to-validate_field_name}

The
`validate_<field_name>`
method hooks that can be attached to serializer classes change their signature slightly and return type. Previously these would take a dictionary of all incoming data, and a key representing the field name, and would return a dictionary including the validated data for that field:

Any ad-hoc validation that applies to more than one field should go in the
`.validate(self, attrs)`
method as usual.

user_input: What's a SerializerMethodField for?
reference: A read-only field whose value comes from a method on the serializer, letting you add arbitrary computed data to the output.
reference_contexts: This is a read-only field. It gets its value by calling a method on the serializer class it is attached to.
llm_response:
A `SerializerMethodField` is a read-only field used to add any sort of data to the serialized representation of an object. It obtains its value by calling a method on the serializer class to which it is attached.

**How it works:**
*   **Method invocation:** By default, the field calls a method named `get_<field_name>` on the serializer. You can specify a different method name using the `method_name` argument.
*   **Method requirements:** The referenced method must accept two arguments: `self` and the object being serialized. It should return the value you want included in the serialized representation.
*   **Consistency:** If you provide a `method_name` that matches the default `get_<field_name>` pattern, an assertion error will be raised to ensure consistent code style.

Signature
:
`SerializerMethodField(method_name=None)`

`method_name`
- The name of the method on the serializer to be called. If not included this defaults to
`get_<field_name>`
.

The serializer method referred to by the
`method_name`
argument should accept a single argument (in addition to
`self`
), which is the object being serialized. It should return whatever you want to be included in the serialized representation of the object. For example:


`fromdjango.contrib.auth.modelsimportUserfromdjango.utils.timezoneimportnowfromrest_frameworkimportserializersclassUserSerializer(serializers.ModelSerializer):days_since_joined=serializers.SerializerMethodField()classMeta:model=Userfields='__all__'defget_days_since_joined(self,obj):return(now()-obj.date_joined).days`

Each serializer field class constructor takes at least these arguments.  Some Field classes take additional, field-specific arguments, but the following should always be accepted:

Read-only fields are included in the API output, but should not be included in the input during create or update operations. Any 'read_only' fields that are incorrectly included in the serializer input will be ignored.

Set this to

Defaults to

Note
There is a special-case where a read-only field is part of a
`unique_together`
constraint at the model level. In this case the field is required by the serializer class in order to validate the constraint, but should also not be editable by the user.
The right way to deal with this is to specify the field explicitly on the serializer, providing both the

One example of this is a read-only relation to the currently authenticated

user_input: How does the source argument on a serializer field work?
reference: source names the attribute used to populate the field; it can be a no-arg method or a dotted path like 'user.email' to traverse relations.
reference_contexts: The name of the attribute that will be used to populate the field.
llm_response:
The `source` argument on a serializer field is used to specify the attribute that will be used to populate the field. It defaults to the name of the field itself [7].

Key points regarding its usage:

*   **Redundancy:** Setting `source` to the same value as the field name is redundant and will raise an error (e.g., `email=serializers.EmailField(source='email')` is not allowed) [4].
*   **Mapping:** It can be used to map a field name to a different attribute name on the source object. For example, `x=serializers.IntegerField(source='x_coordinate')` maps the field `x` to the `x_coordinate` attribute [5].
*   **Special value `*`:** The value `source='*'` indicates that the entire object should be passed to the field. This is useful for nested representations or when a field requires access to the complete object to determine its output [7].
*   **SerializerMethodField:** The `source` argument is also used in `SerializerMethodField` to specify the method name, such as `billing_details=serializers.SerializerMethodField('get_billing_details')` [4].

## Custom relational fields¶ {#custom-relational-fields}

In rare cases where none of the existing relational styles fit the representation you need,
you can implement a completely custom relational field, that describes exactly how the

To implement a custom relational field, you should override
`RelatedField`
, and implement the
`.to_representation(self, value)`
method. This method takes the target of the field as the
`value`
argument, and should return the representation that should be used to serialize the target. The
`value`
argument will typically be a model instance.

If you want to implement a read-write relational field, you must also implement the
.to_internal_value(self, data) method (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/serializers/#to_internal_valueself-data)
.

To authenticate a request in tests without using the real credential flow, use the `force_authenticate()` method.

## What's next?¶ {#whats-next}

Rather than writing your own viewsets, you'll often want to use the existing base classes that provide a default set of behavior.  For example:


`classUserViewSet(viewsets.ModelViewSet):"""
A viewset for viewing and editing user instances.
"""serializer_class=UserSerializerqueryset=User.objects.all()`


There are two main advantages of using a
`ViewSet`
class over using a
`View`
class.

Repeated logic can be combined into a single class.  In the above example, we only need to specify the
`queryset`
once, and it'll be used across multiple views.
By using routers, we no longer need to deal with wiring up the URL conf ourselves.

Both of these come with a trade-off.  Using regular views and URL confs is more explicit and gives you more control.  ViewSets are helpful if you want to get up and running quickly, or when you have a large API and you want to enforce a consistent URL configuration throughout.

`request.data`
returns the parsed content of the request body.  This is similar to the standard
`request.POST`
and
`request.FILES`

and

requests.
It supports REST framework's flexible request parsing, rather than just supporting form data.  For example you can handle incoming

Previously the serializers used a two-step object creation, as follows:

Validating the data would create an object instance. This instance would be available as

Calling
`serializer.save()`

This style is in-line with how the

Note that if you wanted to use this style together with the generic views then you'd also need to override

user_input: What's DRF's reverse() and how does it differ from Django's?
reference: rest_framework.reverse.reverse behaves like django.urls.reverse but returns a fully qualified URL using the request's host/port — so pass the request.
reference_contexts: Signature: reverse(viewname, *args, **kwargs) Has the same behavior as django.urls.reverse , except that it returns a fully qualified URL, using the request to determine the host and port.
llm_response:
DRF's `reverse()` is a utility function that functions similarly to `django.urls.reverse`, with two primary differences:

*   **Fully qualified URLs:** It returns a fully qualified URL by using the provided `request` to determine the host and port.
*   **Versioning integration:** It ties into the API versioning scheme. By including the current `request` as a keyword argument, the function applies URL transformations appropriate to the request's version (e.g., prepending a version prefix like `v1:` or appending a query parameter like `?version=1.0`).

To use these features, you must include the current `request` as a keyword argument:

```python
from rest_framework.reverse import reverse
reverse('view-name', request=request)
```

user_input: What does @api_view do to a plain function view?
reference: It wraps the function so it gets a DRF Request and returns a DRF Response for the listed HTTP methods; by default only GET is accepted and others get a 405.
reference_contexts: By default only GET methods will be accepted. Other methods will respond with "405 Method Not Allowed".
llm_response:
The `@api_view` decorator wraps a function-based view to provide the following functionality:

*   **Request/Response handling:** It ensures the view receives `Request` instances and adds context to `Response` objects to enable content negotiation.
*   **Method handling:** It restricts the view to specific HTTP methods (defaulting to `GET`). If a request is made using an unsupported method, it returns a `405 Method Not Allowed` response.
*   **Error handling:** It handles `ParseError` exceptions that occur when accessing `request.data` with malformed input.
*   **Configuration:** It causes the view to use the default renderers, parsers, and authentication classes specified in the settings.

## Wrapping API views¶ {#wrapping-api-views}

REST framework provides two wrappers you can use to write API views.

The
`@api_view`
decorator for working with function based views.
The
`APIView`
class for working with class-based views.

These wrappers provide a few bits of functionality such as making sure you receive
`Request`
instances in your view, and adding context to
`Response`
objects so that content negotiation can be performed.

The wrappers also provide behavior such as returning
`405 Method Not Allowed`
responses when appropriate, and handling any
`ParseError`
exceptions that occur when accessing
`request.data`
with malformed input.

The DRF-native approach for token-based authentication is `TokenAuthentication`. It is appropriate for mobile clients and does not use server-side sessions.

### Installation and Configuration
To use `TokenAuthentication`, you must perform the following steps:

1.  **Update `INSTALLED_APPS`**: Add `'rest_framework.authtoken'` to your `INSTALLED_APPS` setting.
2.  **Run Migrations**: Execute `manage.py migrate` to apply the migrations provided by the `rest_framework.authtoken` app.
3.  **Configure Authentication**: Configure your authentication classes to include `TokenAuthentication`.

### Generating Tokens
To provide an endpoint that returns a credential (token) given a username and password, you must create tokens for your users. You can do this programmatically using:

```python
from rest_framework.authtoken.models import Token
token = Token.objects.create(user=...)
print(token.key)
```

Alternatively, you can use the management command `./manage.py drf_create_token <username>` to return or create an API token for a specific user.

### Alternatives
While `TokenAuthentication` is the built-in DRF approach, the documentation notes that it is a "fairly simple implementation." For requirements such as token expiry, multiple tokens per user, or tighter security, the documentation recommends the third-party package **Django REST Knox**. Other third-party packages mentioned for handling authentication actions (like login/logout) include **Djoser** and **dj-rest-auth**.

reference: Don't take it from request data. In a generic view override perform_create to save with user=self.request.user, or on the serializer use a HiddenField with default=CurrentUserDefault so the current user is injected at save.

llm_response:
To ensure the owner is set automatically to the logged-in user without the client sending it, you should handle the association in the view rather than the serializer.

The recommended approach is to override the `.perform_create()` method in your view class. This allows you to inject the user from the request into the save process:

```python
def perform_create(self, serializer):
    serializer.save(owner=self.request.user)
```

This method ensures that the `owner` field is passed to the serializer's `create()` method along with the validated data from the request.

Additionally, you must ensure the field is read-only in your serializer so that it is not expected from the client. You can do this by adding the field to your serializer definition:

```python
owner = serializers.ReadOnlyField(source="owner.username")
```

Make sure to also include `'owner'` in the `fields` list of your serializer's `Meta` class.

user_input: My API is getting hammered. I want to cap how many requests anonymous vs logged-in users can make per day. What's the mechanism and where do the numbers go?
reference: Enable AnonRateThrottle and UserRateThrottle as throttle classes and put the actual limits (like '100/day' and '1000/day') under DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES.
reference_contexts: The default throttling policy may be set globally, using the DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES and DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES settings.

REST_FRAMEWORK = { 'DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES' : [ 'rest_framework.throttling.AnonRateThrottle' , 'rest_framework.throttling.UserRateThrottle' ], 'DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES' : { 'anon' : '100/day' , 'user' : '1000/day' } } The rates used in DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES can be specified over a period of second, minute, hour or day.
A list or tuple of throttle classes, that determines the default set of throttles checked at the start of a view.
llm_response:
To cap requests for anonymous and logged-in users, you use the `AnonRateThrottle` and `UserRateThrottle` classes. You can apply these to your views using the `@throttle_classes` decorator or by setting the `throttle_classes` attribute on `APIView` subclasses.

### Where the numbers go
The allowed request rates are determined by the following mechanisms, listed in order of preference:

1.  **Class Property:** You can override the `AnonRateThrottle` or `UserRateThrottle` classes and set a `rate` property directly on the class (e.g., `rate = '1/day'`).
2.  **Settings:** You can define the rates in your project's `REST_FRAMEWORK` settings using the `DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES` dictionary. Specifically:
    *   For anonymous users: Use the `'anon'` key (e.g., `'DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES': {'anon': '100/day'}`).
    *   For logged-in users: Use the `'user'` key (e.g., `'DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES': {'user': '1000/day'}`).

### How it works
*   **`AnonRateThrottle`**: Used to restrict requests from unknown sources.
*   **`UserRateThrottle`**: Throttles users based on their user ID. If a request is unauthenticated, it falls back to using the IP address to generate a unique key for throttling.

You can use multiple throttles simultaneously to apply different constraints to different types of users.

# Throttling¶ {#throttling}

HTTP/1.1 420 Enhance Your Calm
Twitter API rate limiting response (https://developer.twitter.com/en/docs/basics/rate-limiting)

Throttling is similar to
permissions (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/permissions/)
, in that it determines if a request should be authorized.  Throttles indicate a temporary state, and are used to control the rate of requests that clients can make to an API.

As with permissions, multiple throttles may be used.  Your API might have a restrictive throttle for unauthenticated requests, and a less restrictive throttle for authenticated requests.

Another scenario where you might want to use multiple throttles would be if you need to impose different constraints on different parts of the API, due to some services being particularly resource-intensive.

Multiple throttles can also be used if you want to impose both burst throttling rates, and sustained throttling rates.  For example, you might want to limit a user to a maximum of 60 requests per minute, and 1000 requests per day.

Throttles do not necessarily only refer to rate-limiting requests.  For example a storage service might also need to throttle against bandwidth, and a paid data service might want to throttle against a certain number of a records being accessed.

The application-level throttling that REST framework provides should not be considered a security measure or protection against brute forcing or denial-of-service attacks. Deliberately malicious actors will always be able to spoof IP origins. In addition to this, the built-in throttling implementations are implemented using Django's cache framework, and use non-atomic operations to determine the request rate, which may sometimes result in some fuzziness.

user_input: Scrapers hit us in short violent bursts; our real users trickle requests out over the whole day. If I set the ceiling low enough to stop a burst I punish the real users, and if I set it high enough for the real users the bursts sail through. Can I enforce both shapes at once?
reference: Yes — stack two throttles instead of picking one number. Subclass UserRateThrottle twice and give each subclass its own unique `scope`, e.g. a `burst` class and a `sustained` class, then list both in DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES and define a rate for each scope under DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES (something like '60/min' and '1000/day'). Multiple UserRateThrottles can be in force at the same time, and every request is checked against all of them, so a client has to stay under the short window and the long one simultaneously.

llm_response:
Yes, you can enforce both burst and sustained rates at the same time by using multiple throttles.

To implement this, you should override `UserRateThrottle` to create separate classes for each rate and assign them unique scopes.

### Implementation Steps:

1. **Define the throttle classes:**
   Create classes for your burst and sustained rates:
   ```python
   class BurstRateThrottle(UserRateThrottle):
       scope = 'burst'

   class SustainedRateThrottle(UserRateThrottle):
       scope = 'sustained'
   ```

2. **Configure the settings:**
   Add these classes to your `DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES` and define the corresponding rates in `DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES`:
   ```python
   REST_FRAMEWORK = {
       'DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES': [
           'example.throttles.BurstRateThrottle',
           'example.throttles.SustainedRateThrottle'
       ],
       'DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES': {
           'burst': '60/min',
           'sustained': '1000/day'
       }
   }
   ```

By including both classes in `DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES`, the API will apply both restrictions simultaneously.

### ScopedRateThrottle¶ {#scopedratethrottle}

The
`ScopedRateThrottle`

user_input: When the payment provider we call during checkout is slow or down, our endpoint currently returns a wall of HTML with a stack trace in it. I want it to answer with a clean, machine-readable 'try again shortly' that our clients can branch on, and I want to define that once rather than writing the same try/except into every view that touches the provider.
reference: Define your own exception type and raise it; the framework turns it into the response. Subclass APIException — the base class for exceptions raised inside an APIView or @api_view — and set `.status_code`, `.default_detail` and `.default_code` on the class, e.g. a ServiceUnavailable with status_code = 503 and a default_detail of 'Service temporarily unavailable, try again later.'. Then any view that raises it produces that response, handled centrally instead of per view, and the body comes back in the standard error shape with a `detail` key rather than as a Django HTML error page. Note the boundary: this handling only applies to responses generated by *raised* exceptions — a Response object you return directly from a view, such as an explicit HTTP_400_BAD_REQUEST, never passes through it.

Subclasses of APIException raised inside REST framework.

llm_response:
To handle the slow or down payment provider with a clean, machine-readable response, you should implement a custom exception by subclassing `APIException`.

### Implementation
1. **Define the custom exception:** Create a class that inherits from `APIException` and set the `status_code`, `default_detail`, and `default_code` attributes. As shown in the documentation:

   ```python
   from rest_framework.exceptions import APIException

   class ServiceUnavailable(APIException):
       status_code = 503
       default_detail = 'Service temporarily unavailable, try again later.'
       default_code = 'service_unavailable'
   ```

2. **Custom Exception Handling:** To define this behavior once for your application rather than writing try/except blocks in every view, you can write a custom exception handler. The documentation notes that you can implement custom exception handling for your project by using the properties available for inspecting API exceptions.

### Note on Debugging
The documentation specifies that if `DEBUG=True`, Django's standard traceback error page will be displayed instead of the rendered HTTP status code and text. Ensure `DEBUG` is set to `False` in your environment to see the machine-readable response.

reference: You don't need a second serializer class — the field set is mutable at runtime. Once a serializer is initialized its fields are available as the `.fields` attribute, an ordinary dictionary you can read and modify, which lets you change what gets rendered (and the arguments on individual fields) per instance rather than at declaration time. The documented pattern is a DynamicFieldsModelSerializer: accept an extra `fields` keyword in __init__, pop it before calling super(), and then drop everything not requested from self.fields. Your view decides what to pass — typically driven by a query parameter — so UserSerializer(user) returns the full record and UserSerializer(user, fields=('id', 'email')) returns the narrow one from the same class and the same URL. If you'd rather not hand-roll it, drf-dynamic-fields provides a mixin that limits fields from a URL parameter, and drf-flex-fields additionally handles expanding primitive fields into nested ones.
reference_contexts: Once a serializer has been initialized, the dictionary of fields that are set on the serializer may be accessed using the .fields attribute. Accessing and modifying this attribute allows you to dynamically modify the serializer.
Modifying the fields argument directly allows you to do interesting things such as changing the arguments on serializer fields at runtime, rather than at the point of declaring the serializer.

class DynamicFieldsModelSerializer(serializers.ModelSerializer): """ A ModelSerializer that takes an additional `fields` argument that controls which fields should be displayed. """ def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs): # Don't pass the 'fields' arg up to the superclass fields = kwargs.pop('fields', None) # Instantiate the superclass normally super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
print(UserSerializer(user)) {'id': 2, 'username': 'jonwatts', 'email': 'jon@example.com'} print(UserSerializer(user, fields=('id', 'email'))) {'id': 2, 'email': 'jon@example.com'}
The drf-dynamic-fields package provides a mixin to dynamically limit the fields per serializer to a subset specified by an URL parameter.

llm_response:
To set up a self-describing API that is browsable in a browser while maintaining JSON as the primary format, you should configure the `DEFAULT_RENDERER_CLASSES` in your `REST_FRAMEWORK` settings.

Include both `JSONRenderer` and `BrowsableAPIRenderer` in the list, placing `JSONRenderer` first to ensure it is the main media type:

```python
REST_FRAMEWORK = {
    'DEFAULT_RENDERER_CLASSES': [
        'rest_framework.renderers.JSONRenderer',
        'rest_framework.renderers.BrowsableAPIRenderer',
    ]
}
```

This configuration allows the API to return a web-browsable HTML representation when requested by a browser, while defaulting to JSON for other requests. You can also apply these renderers to individual views or viewsets if preferred.

user_input: I'm tired of writing near-identical URL patterns for every model's list and detail views. What's the DRF way to cut that boilerplate?
reference: Move to ViewSets and let a router generate URLs: register each ViewSet with a router and include router.urls, which keeps URL conventions consistent and removes hand-written patterns.
reference_contexts: The conventions for wiring up resources into views and urls can be handled automatically, using a Router class.

It helps ensure that URL conventions will be consistent across your API, minimizes the amount of code you need to write, and allows you to concentrate on the interactions and representations your API provides rather than the specifics of the URL conf.

Also note that although this class provides the complete set of create/list/retrieve/update/destroy actions by default, you can restrict the available operations by using the standard permission classes.
REST framework adds support for automatic URL routing to Django, and provides you with a simple, quick and consistent way of wiring your view logic to a set of URLs.
llm_response:
To cut boilerplate for model list and detail views, you should use **ViewSets** and a **Router**.

Instead of writing individual URL patterns for every view, you can group common behavior into a `ViewSet` and use a router to automatically generate the URL configuration.

### How to implement:
1.  **Use a Router:** Register your viewsets with a router class (such as `DefaultRouter`). This automatically generates the URL patterns for your API.
    ```python
    from rest_framework import routers
    from myapp import views

    router = routers.DefaultRouter()
    router.register(r"users", views.UserViewSet)
    router.register(r"accounts", views.AccountViewSet)

    urlpatterns = [
        path("", include(router.urls)),
    ]
    ```
    This will automatically generate patterns like `^users/$` (named `'user-list'`) and `^users/{pk}/$` (named `'user-detail'`).

2.  **Handle `basename`:** If your viewset does not have a `.queryset` attribute (e.g., you defined a custom `get_queryset` method), you must explicitly provide the `basename` argument when registering the viewset:
    ```python
    router.register(r"users", views.UserViewSet, basename="user")
    ```

3.  **Generic Views:** For building API views that map closely to your database models, you can also use the pre-built **Generic views** provided by the REST framework, which abstract common idioms and patterns to reduce repetition.

# Generic views¶ {#generic-views}

Django’s generic views... were developed as a shortcut for common usage patterns... They take certain common idioms and patterns found in view development and abstract them so that you can quickly write common views of data without having to repeat yourself.
—
Django Documentation (https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/ref/class-based-views/#base-vs-generic-views)

One of the key benefits of class-based views is the way they allow you to compose bits of reusable behavior.  REST framework takes advantage of this by providing a number of pre-built views that provide for commonly used patterns.

The generic views provided by REST framework allow you to quickly build API views that map closely to your database models.

Rather than write multiple views we're grouping together all the common behavior into classes called
`ViewSets`
.

We can easily break these down into individual views if we need to, but using viewsets keeps the view logic nicely organized as well as being very concise.

## URLs¶ {#urls}

Okay, now let's wire up the API URLs.  On to
`tutorial/urls.py`
...


`fromdjango.urlsimportinclude,pathfromrest_frameworkimportroutersfromtutorial.quickstartimportviewsrouter=routers.DefaultRouter()router.register(r"users",views.UserViewSet)router.register(r"groups",views.GroupViewSet)# Wire up our API using automatic URL routing.# Additionally, we include login URLs for the browsable API.urlpatterns=[path("",include(router.urls)),path("api-auth/",include("rest_framework.urls",namespace="rest_framework")),]`


Because we're using viewsets instead of views, we can automatically generate the URL conf for our API, by simply registering the viewsets with a router class.

llm_response:
To address the performance issue with the browsable API form when dealing with a large number of items, you have the following options:

**1. Use a standard text input (Recommended for simplicity)**
You can replace the select input widget with a standard text input. This prevents the browser from attempting to render all 80,000 rows. You do this by setting the `style` argument on the field:
`author = serializers.HyperlinkedRelatedField(queryset=User.objects.all(), style={'base_template': 'input.html'})`

**2. Rely on the default select field cutoff**
Relational fields in the browsable API have a built-in mechanism to prevent performance issues by defaulting to a maximum of 1,000 selectable items. If more than 1,000 items are present, the system displays a disabled option labeled "More than 1000 items…" instead of rendering the entire list. You can control this behavior using two keyword arguments (though the specific names of these arguments are not provided in the excerpts).

To version the behavior of a view in Django REST framework, you can use the `request.version` attribute, which contains a string corresponding to the version requested by the client.

### How to vary behavior
You can vary the API behavior by checking the `request.version` attribute within your view methods. A common approach is to switch serialization styles based on the version. For example:

```python
def get_serializer_class(self):
    if self.request.version == 'v1':
        return AccountSerializerVersion1
    return AccountSerializer
```

### Versioning Schemes
REST framework provides built-in schemes for versioning, which are determined by the incoming request:
*   **Accept header based:** Generally considered best practice.
*   **URL based:** Includes schemes such as `NamespaceVersioning`.

When using URL-based versioning, hyperlinked serializers will automatically resolve relationships to the same API version used in the incoming request, provided you include the request as context to the serializer.

### Reversing URLs
When reversing URLs for versioned APIs, you must include the current `request` as a keyword argument to the `reverse` function:

```python
from rest_framework.reverse import reverse
reverse('bookings-list', request=request)
```

This ensures the function applies the URL transformations appropriate to the request version (e.g., resolving to `'v1:bookings-list'` or appending a query parameter like `?version=1.0`).

To expose an extra custom action on a viewset, decorate the method with the `@action` decorator. 

You must set the `detail` argument to `True` if the action is intended for a single object (such as a 'highlight' endpoint for a specific snippet) or `False` if it is intended for an entire collection. The router will then automatically configure the URL patterns accordingly, including the `pk` in the URL for detail actions.

Example:

```python
from rest_framework.decorators import action

class SnippetViewSet(viewsets.ModelViewSet):
    ...
    @action(detail=True, methods=['get'])
    def highlight(self, request, pk=None):
        ...
```

By default, the `@action` decorator routes `GET` requests, but you can specify other HTTP methods using the `methods` argument (e.g., `methods=['post']`).

llm_response:
To render real HTML pages using your own templates, you should use `TemplateHTMLRenderer`.

### How it works
When using `TemplateHTMLRenderer`, the view returns a `Response` object containing the data (context) to be rendered. You must specify the template to be used, which is determined by the following order of preference:
1. An explicit `template_name` argument passed to the `Response`.
2. An explicit `.template_name` attribute set on the view class.
3. The return result of calling `view.get_template_names()`.

**Example:**
```python
class UserDetail(generics.RetrieveAPIView):
    queryset = User.objects.all()
    renderer_classes = [TemplateHTMLRenderer]

    def get(self, request, *args, **kwargs):
        self.object = self.get_object()
        return Response({'user': self.object}, template_name='user_detail.html')
```

### Alternative
If you do not need to use templates and instead want to return pre-rendered HTML, you can use `StaticHTMLRenderer`. In this case, the view returns a `Response` object where the data is a string representing the HTML content.

## Ordering of renderer classes¶ {#ordering-of-renderer-classes}

It's important when specifying the renderer classes for your API to think about what priority you want to assign to each media type.  If a client underspecifies the representations it can accept, such as sending an
`Accept: */*`
header, or not including an
`Accept`
header at all, then REST framework will select the first renderer in the list to use for the response.

For example if your API serves JSON responses and the HTML browsable API, you might want to make
`JSONRenderer`
your default renderer, in order to send
`JSON`
responses to clients that do not specify an
`Accept`
header.

If your API includes views that can serve both regular webpages and API responses depending on the request, then you might consider making
`TemplateHTMLRenderer`
your default renderer, in order to play nicely with older browsers that send
broken accept headers (http://www.gethifi.com/blog/browser-rest-http-accept-headers)
.

To accept a raw file upload, set the `parser_classes` on your API view to `FileUploadParser`. Because its `media_type` matches any content type (`*/*`), it should generally be the only parser set on the view.

2.  **HTTP Header:** If no `filename` URL keyword argument is provided, the client must set the filename in the `Content-Disposition` HTTP header (e.g., `Content-Disposition: attachment; filename=upload.jpg`).

llm_response:
Yes, you can combine permission classes using the `|` (OR) operator. 

As shown in the documentation, you can compose permissions directly within the `permission_classes` list using the `|` (or), `&` (and), and `~` (not) operators, along with brackets `()` to group expressions.

For example, to combine `IsAuthenticated` and a custom `ReadOnly` permission:

```python
from rest_framework.permissions import IsAuthenticated, SAFE_METHODS, BasePermission

class ReadOnly(BasePermission):
    def has_permission(self, request, view):
        return request.method in SAFE_METHODS

class ExampleView(APIView):
    permission_classes = [IsAuthenticated | ReadOnly]
```

Additionally, for the specific case of allowing authenticated users read-write access and unauthenticated users read-only access, the framework provides a built-in class called `IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly`.

To page through a huge, constantly-growing table efficiently while ensuring clients never see duplicates when rows are inserted, you should use **`CursorPagination`**.

### Why `CursorPagination`
*   **Efficiency:** Unlike offset-based pagination, which can become inefficient or unusable with extremely large datasets, `CursorPagination` has fixed-time properties and does not slow down as the dataset size increases.
*   **No Duplicates:** When used properly, it ensures that a client will never see the same item twice, even if new items are inserted by other clients during the pagination process.

### The Catch
`CursorPagination` is more complex than other schemes and comes with the following limitations:
*   **No Arbitrary Indexing:** It does not allow the client to navigate to arbitrary positions (e.g., jumping to page 50); it only provides forward and reverse controls.
*   **Ordering Requirements:** It requires a unique, unchanging ordering of items. The ordering field must:
    *   Be an unchanging value (e.g., a timestamp, slug, or other field set only once on creation).
    *   Be unique or nearly unique (millisecond precision timestamps are recommended).
    *   Be non-nullable and capable of being coerced to a string.
    *   Not be a float (to avoid precision errors).
    *   Have a database index.
*   **Configuration:** You must define the ordering you want the scheme to be applied against (the default is `"-created"`).

### Browsability¶ {#browsability}

Provides a consistent pagination view. When used properly
`CursorPagination`
ensures that the client will never see the same item twice when paging through records, even when new items are being inserted by other clients during the pagination process.
Supports usage with very large datasets. With extremely large datasets pagination using offset-based pagination styles may become inefficient or unusable. Cursor based pagination schemes instead have fixed-time properties, and do not slow down as the dataset size increases.

#### Details and limitations¶ {#details-and-limitations}

Proper use of cursor based pagination requires a little attention to detail. You'll need to think about what ordering you want the scheme to be applied against. The default is to order by
`"-created"`
. This assumes that
there must be a 'created' timestamp field
on the model instances, and will present a "timeline" style paginated view, with the most recently added items first.

### CursorPagination¶ {#cursorpagination}

The cursor-based pagination presents an opaque "cursor" indicator that the client may use to page through the result set. This pagination style only presents forward and reverse controls, and does not allow the client to navigate to arbitrary positions.

Cursor based pagination requires that there is a unique, unchanging ordering of items in the result set. This ordering might typically be a creation timestamp on the records, as this presents a consistent ordering to paginate against.

Cursor based pagination is more complex than other schemes. It also requires that the result set presents a fixed ordering, and does not allow the client to arbitrarily index into the result set. However it does provide the following benefits:

Proper usage of cursor pagination should have an ordering field that satisfies the following:

Should be an unchanging value, such as a timestamp, slug, or other field that is only set once, on creation.
Should be unique, or nearly unique. Millisecond precision timestamps are a good example. This implementation of cursor pagination uses a smart "position plus offset" style that allows it to properly support not-strictly-unique values as the ordering.
Should be a non-nullable value that can be coerced to a string.
Should not be a float. Precision errors easily lead to incorrect results.
Hint: use decimals instead.
(If you already have a float field and must paginate on that, an
example CursorPagination subclass that uses decimals to limit precision is available here (https://gist.github.com/keturn/8bc88525a183fd41c73ffb729b8865be#file-fpcursorpagination-py)
.)
The field should have a database index.

### LimitOffsetPagination¶ {#limitoffsetpagination}

This pagination style mirrors the syntax used when looking up multiple database records. The client includes both a "limit" and an
"offset" query parameter. The limit indicates the maximum number of items to return, and is equivalent to the
`page_size`
in other styles. The offset indicates the starting position of the query in relation to the complete set of unpaginated items.

Request
:


`GET https://api.example.org/accounts/?limit=100&offset=400`


Response
:


`HTTP200OK{"count":1023,"next":"https://api.example.org/accounts/?limit=100&offset=500","previous":"https://api.example.org/accounts/?limit=100&offset=300","results":[…]}`


#### Setup¶ {#setup_1}

To enable the
`LimitOffsetPagination`
style globally, use the following configuration:


`REST_FRAMEWORK={'DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS':'rest_framework.pagination.LimitOffsetPagination'}`

llm_response:
To prevent a user from creating two records with the same combination of two fields, you should use the `UniqueTogetherValidator`. This validator is applied to the `Meta` class of your serializer.

You must provide two required arguments:
*   `queryset`: The queryset against which uniqueness is enforced.
*   `fields`: A list or tuple of the field names that should make up the unique set.

As shown in the documentation, you implement it like this:

```python
from rest_framework.validators import UniqueTogetherValidator

class ExampleSerializer(serializers.Serializer):
    # ...
    class Meta:
        validators = [
            UniqueTogetherValidator(
                queryset=ToDoItem.objects.all(),
                fields=['list', 'position']
            )
        ]
```

**Important considerations:**
*   **Required Fields:** The `UniqueTogetherValidator` imposes an implicit constraint that all fields it applies to are required. If a field has a `default` value, it is an exception to this rule [4].
*   **Read-Only Fields:** If a field involved in a `unique_together` constraint is read-only (such as a user field), you must explicitly declare the field on the serializer with `read_only=True` and provide a `default` value (e.g., `serializers.CurrentUserDefault()`) to ensure the validator can still perform its check [7].

user_input: When should I reach for a ReadOnlyModelViewSet instead of a full ModelViewSet, and what do the two actually differ on?
reference: Use ReadOnlyModelViewSet when you only need read endpoints: it provides just .list() and .retrieve(), whereas ModelViewSet gives the full create/list/retrieve/update/destroy set. Both inherit from GenericAPIView and both still require queryset and serializer_class.
reference_contexts: all () serializer_class = UserSerializer Here we've used the ReadOnlyModelViewSet class to automatically provide the default 'read-only' operations.
We're still setting the queryset and serializer_class attributes exactly as we did when we were using regular views, but we no longer need to provide the same information to two separate classes.
The ModelViewSet class inherits from GenericAPIView and includes implementations for various actions, by mixing in the behavior of the various mixin classes.
The ReadOnlyModelViewSet class also inherits from GenericAPIView .
llm_response:
You should reach for a `ReadOnlyModelViewSet` when you want to provide only 'read-only' actions for a model.

The two classes differ in the following ways:

*   **`ModelViewSet`**: Provides the complete set of actions by default: `.list()`, `.retrieve()`, `.create()`, `.update()`, `.partial_update()`, and `.destroy()`.
*   **`ReadOnlyModelViewSet`**: Provides only the 'read-only' actions: `.list()` and `.retrieve()`.

While `ModelViewSet` provides all operations by default, you can restrict available operations on it by using standard permission classes. Both classes inherit from `GenericAPIView` and typically require you to provide at least the `queryset` and `serializer_class` attributes.

user_input: When an unauthenticated request is rejected I sometimes get 401 and sometimes 403. What actually decides which one DRF returns?
reference: It hinges on whether the first/highest-priority authentication class uses a WWW-Authenticate header: if it does, an unauthenticated denial is 401 with that header; if not, it's 403. A request that authenticated but lacked permission is always 403.
reference_contexts: The first authentication class set on the view is used when determining the type of response .
The request was not successfully authenticated, and the highest priority authentication class does not use WWW-Authenticate headers.
HTTP 401 Unauthorized HTTP 403 Permission Denied HTTP 401 responses must always include a WWW-Authenticate header, that instructs the client how to authenticate.
Signature: AuthenticationFailed(detail=None, code=None) Raised when an incoming request includes incorrect authentication.
llm_response:
Whether DRF returns a 401 or 403 response when an unauthenticated request is rejected depends on the following rules:

*   **403 Forbidden:** This is returned if the request was successfully authenticated but permission was denied, or if the request was not successfully authenticated and the highest priority authentication class **does not** use `WWW-Authenticate` headers.
*   **401 Unauthorized:** This is returned if the request was not successfully authenticated and the highest priority authentication class **does** use `WWW-Authenticate` headers.

The use of `WWW-Authenticate` headers is determined by the authentication scheme:
*   If the `.authenticate_header(self, request)` method is implemented in the authentication scheme, it returns the string used for the `WWW-Authenticate` header, resulting in a 401 response.
*   If the `.authenticate_header()` method is not overridden, the authentication scheme will return 403 responses when an unauthenticated request is denied access.

reference: Schema generation is two layers, and your two symptoms come from different ones. SchemaGenerator is the top-level piece: it walks your configured URL patterns, finds the APIView subclasses behind them, asks each one for its schema representation, and compiles the result — so anything not reachable through the URL conf simply isn't seen, which is the first thing to check for the missing actions. The per-view detail comes from AutoSchema, which is attached to each view through its `schema` attribute and does the introspection; you subclass AutoSchema to customise what a view reports, and set a project-wide default with the DEFAULT_SCHEMA_CLASS setting. An endpoint comes out blank rather than wrong when the introspection has nothing to infer from — there's no serializer for it to read — which is why the docs tell you to annotate the generated schema with any additional information that cannot be automatically inferred. Worth knowing before you invest in this: the built-in schema support is deprecated in favour of third-party packages, and drf-spectacular is the recommended full replacement.

llm_response:
Based on the provided documentation, here is how the three methods control access for list and create actions:

### **1. `queryset` / `get_queryset()`**
*   **List:** Provides global control by limiting the visibility of existing objects from the database. It is the recommended way to ensure users only see instances they are permitted to view, as generic views do not automatically apply object-level permissions to each instance in a list.
*   **Create:** Does not apply.
*   **Note:** By using `get_queryset()`, you can return different querysets based on the current action or request.

### **2. `permission_classes` / `get_permissions()`**
*   **List:** Provides global permission checks applied to the entire object type.
*   **Create:** Provides global permission checks applied to the entire object type.
*   **Note:** Object-level permissions (via `has_object_permission()`) are not applied when creating objects because `get_object()` is not called. To restrict creation, you must implement the check in your serializer or override `perform_create()` in your ViewSet. You can reference the request and action when making decisions.

### **3. `serializer_class` / `get_serializer()`**
*   **List:** Provides object-level restrictions on input and output. However, a serializer should not raise `PermissionDenied` during a list action, or the entire list will fail to return.
*   **Create:** Provides object-level restrictions on input.
*   **Note:** Serializers have access to the request context. You can use `get_serializer()` to apply different serializers based on the current action.

### **Summary Table**

| Action | `queryset` | `permission_classes` | `serializer_class` |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **List** | Global | Global | Object-level* |
| **Create** | No | Global | Object-level |

*\*A Serializer class should not raise PermissionDenied in a list action.*

Currently our API doesn't have any restrictions on who can edit or delete code snippets.  We'd like to have some more advanced behavior in order to make sure that:

Code snippets are always associated with a creator.
Only authenticated users may create snippets.
Only the creator of a snippet may update or delete it.
Unauthenticated requests should have full read-only access.

The `reverse` function in REST framework integrates with the versioning scheme by applying URL transformations appropriate to the version of the incoming request [1, 4].

To ensure reversed URLs point to the correct version, you must pass the current `request` as a keyword argument to the `reverse` function [1, 4, 6].

**Example usage:**
```python
from rest_framework.reverse import reverse
reverse('bookings-list', request=request)
```

When this is done, the function will correctly apply the versioning scheme (such as `NamespaceVersioning` or `QueryParameterVersioning`) to the generated URL [1]. Additionally, if you are using hyperlinked serialization styles with a URL-based versioning scheme, you must also include the `request` as context to the serializer [1].

user_input: I want per-view control over both the authentication scheme and the permissions on one endpoint. How do these relate and how do I set both on one APIView?
reference: They're separate but sequential: authentication identifies the request and runs first (setting request.user/request.auth), then permissions use that to allow or deny. Set authentication_classes and permission_classes together — authentication alone never grants access.
reference_contexts: Note Don't forget that authentication by itself won't allow or disallow an incoming request , it simply identifies the credentials that the request was made with.
Permission checks will typically use the authentication information in the request.user and request.auth properties to determine if the incoming request should be permitted.
— Apple Developer Documentation Together with authentication and throttling , permissions determine whether a request should be granted or denied access.
HTTP/1.1 420 Enhance Your Calm Twitter API rate limiting response Throttling is similar to permissions , in that it determines if a request should be authorized.
llm_response:
To set per-view control over both the authentication scheme and permissions on an `APIView`, you define the `authentication_classes` and `permission_classes` attributes directly on your class.

### How to set them
You assign a list of the desired classes to each attribute within your `APIView` subclass. For example:

```python
from rest_framework.views import APIView
from rest_framework import authentication, permissions

class ExampleView(APIView):
    authentication_classes = [authentication.TokenAuthentication]
    permission_classes = [permissions.IsAdminUser]

    def get(self, request, format=None):
        # View logic here
        pass
```

### How they relate
Authentication and permission classes are used by the REST framework to determine access to the view. Authentication is determined first, identifying the user (or the credentials provided), while permissions are used to determine whether that request should be permitted or denied based on the identity established by the authentication scheme. 

While these can be set globally via `DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES` and `DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES` in your settings, setting them as attributes on an `APIView` overrides the global defaults for that specific endpoint.

decorator for working with function based views.

#### Removal of view attributes.¶ {#removal-of-view-attributes}

The
`.object`
and
`.object_list`
attributes are no longer set on the view instance. Treating views as mutable object instances that store state during the processing of the view tends to be poor design, and can lead to obscure flow logic.

I would personally recommend that developers treat view instances as immutable objects in their application code.

Allowing

## The hypermedia approach¶ {#the-hypermedia-approach}

To be fully RESTful an API should present its available actions as hypermedia controls in the responses that it sends.

In this approach, rather than documenting the available API endpoints up front, the description instead concentrates on the
media types
that are used.  The available actions that may be taken on any given URL are not strictly fixed, but are instead made available by the presence of link and form controls in the returned document.

To implement a hypermedia API you'll need to decide on an appropriate media type for the API, and implement a custom renderer and parser for that media type.  The
REST, Hypermedia & HATEOAS (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/topics/rest-hypermedia-hateoas/)
section of the documentation includes pointers to background reading, as well as links to various hypermedia formats.

## Django 5.1+LoginRequiredMiddleware¶ {#django-51-loginrequiredmiddleware}

If you're running Django 5.1+ and use the
LoginRequiredMiddleware (https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/ref/middleware/#django.contrib.auth.middleware.LoginRequiredMiddleware)
, please note that all views from DRF are opted-out of this middleware.  This is because the authentication in DRF is based on authentication and permissions classes, which may be determined after the middleware has been applied.  Additionally, when the request is not authenticated, the middleware redirects the user to the login page, which is not suitable for API requests, where it's preferable to return a 401 status code.

REST framework offers an equivalent mechanism for DRF views via the global settings,
`DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES`
and
`DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES`
.  They should be changed accordingly if you need to enforce that API requests are logged in.

## Setting the permission policy¶ {#setting-the-permission-policy}

The default permission policy may be set globally, using the
`DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES`
setting.  For example.


`REST_FRAMEWORK={'DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES':['rest_framework.permissions.IsAuthenticated',]}`


If not specified, this setting defaults to allowing unrestricted access:


`'DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES':['rest_framework.permissions.AllowAny',]`


You can also set the authentication policy on a per-view, or per-viewset basis,
using the
`APIView`
class-based views.


`fromrest_framework.permissionsimportIsAuthenticatedfromrest_framework.responseimportResponsefromrest_framework.viewsimportAPIViewclassExampleView(APIView):permission_classes=[IsAuthenticated]defget(self,request,format=None):content={'status':'request was permitted'}returnResponse(content)`


Or, if you're using the
`@api_view`
decorator with function based views.

Using the
`APIView`
class is pretty much the same as using a regular
`View`
class, as usual, the incoming request is dispatched to an appropriate handler method such as
`.get()`
or
`.post()`
.  Additionally, a number of attributes may be set on the class that control various aspects of the API policy.

For example:


`fromrest_framework.viewsimportAPIViewfromrest_framework.responseimportResponsefromrest_frameworkimportauthentication,permissionsfromdjango.contrib.auth.modelsimportUserclassListUsers(APIView):"""
View to list all users in the system.
* Requires token authentication.
* Only admin users are able to access this view.
"""authentication_classes=[authentication.TokenAuthentication]permission_classes=[permissions.IsAdminUser]defget(self,request,format=None):"""
Return a list of all users.
"""usernames=[user.usernameforuserinUser.objects.all()]returnResponse(usernames)`

`DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES`
setting.  For example.


`REST_FRAMEWORK={'DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES':['rest_framework.authentication.BasicAuthentication','rest_framework.authentication.SessionAuthentication',]}`

#### Usingserializers.ValidationError.¶ {#using-serializersvalidationerror}

Previously
`serializers.ValidationError`
error was simply a synonym for
`django.core.exceptions.ValidationError`
. This has now been altered so that it inherits from the standard
`APIException`
base class.

The reason behind this is that Django's
`ValidationError`
class is intended for use with HTML forms and its API makes using it slightly awkward with nested validation errors that can occur in serializers.

For most users this change shouldn't require any updates to your codebase, but it is worth ensuring that whenever raising validation errors you should prefer using the
`serializers.ValidationError`
exception class, and not Django's built-in exception.

We strongly recommend that you use the namespaced import style of
`import serializers`
and not
`from serializers import ValidationError`
in order to avoid any potential confusion.

#### Using.is_valid(raise_exception=True)¶ {#using-is_validraise_exceptiontrue}

The
`.is_valid()`
method now takes an optional boolean flag,
`raise_exception`
.

Calling
`.is_valid(raise_exception=True)`
will cause a
`ValidationError`
to be raised if the serializer data contains validation errors. This error will be handled by REST framework's default exception handler, allowing you to remove error response handling from your view code.

The handling and formatting of error responses may be altered globally by using the
`EXCEPTION_HANDLER`
settings key.

This change also means it's now possible to alter the style of error responses used by the built-in generic views, without having to include mixin classes or other overrides.

To inject the current user and run extra validation right before the database write in a generic view, you should use the `perform_create(self, serializer)` hook (for creating objects) or the `perform_update(self, serializer)` hook (for updating objects).

You can inject the user and perform validation within these hooks as follows:

```python
def perform_create(self, serializer):
    # Perform additional validation
    if not some_condition:
        raise ValidationError("Your validation error message")
    
    # Inject the current user at save
    serializer.save(user=self.request.user)
```

**Behavior of raising a `ValidationError`:**
Raising a `ValidationError()` within these hooks allows you to provide additional validation logic that applies specifically at the point of the database save.

#### Passing additional attributes to.save()¶ {#passing-additional-attributes-to-save}

Sometimes you'll want your view code to be able to inject additional data at the point of saving the instance. This additional data might include information like the current user, the current time, or anything else that is not part of the request data.

You can do so by including additional keyword arguments when calling
`.save()`
. For example:


`serializer.save(owner=request.user)`


Any additional keyword arguments will be included in the
`validated_data`
argument when
`.create()`
or
`.update()`
are called.

Or use it to serialize multiple instances:


`@api_view(['GET'])defall_high_scores(request):queryset=HighScore.objects.order_by('-score')serializer=HighScoreSerializer(queryset,many=True)returnResponse(serializer.data)`


##### Read-writeBaseSerializerclasses.¶ {#read-write-baseserializer-classes}

To create a read-write serializer we first need to implement a
`.to_internal_value()`
method. This method returns the validated values that will be used to construct the object instance, and may raise a
`ValidationError`
if the supplied data is in an incorrect format.

Once you've implemented
`.to_internal_value()`
, the basic validation API will be available on the serializer, and you will be able to use
`.is_valid()`
,
`.validated_data`
and
`.errors`
.

If you want to also support
`.save()`
you'll need to also implement either or both of the
`.create()`
and
`.update()`
methods.

For example the following code
is no longer valid
:


`ifserializer.is_valid():name=serializer.object.name# Inspect validated field data.logging.info('Creating ticket "%s"'%name)serializer.object.user=request.user# Include the user when saving.serializer.save()`


Instead of using
`.object`
to inspect a partially constructed instance, you would now use
`.validated_data`
to inspect the cleaned incoming values. Also you can't set extra attributes on the instance directly, but instead pass them to the
`.save()`
method as keyword arguments.

The corresponding code would now look like this:


`ifserializer.is_valid():name=serializer.validated_data['name']# Inspect validated field data.logging.info('Creating ticket "%s"'%name)serializer.save(user=request.user)# Include the user when saving.`


#### Using.is_valid(raise_exception=True)¶ {#using-is_validraise_exceptiontrue}

The
`.is_valid()`
method now takes an optional boolean flag,
`raise_exception`
.

reference: Both sides must agree: on the view, lookup_field is the model field used for object lookup (default 'pk'), and for hyperlinked APIs you must make sure both the API views and the serializer classes set the lookup fields when using a custom value.
reference_contexts: lookup_field - The model field that should be used for performing object lookup of individual model instances.
Note that when using hyperlinked APIs you'll need to ensure that both the API views and the serializer classes set the lookup fields if you need to use a custom value.
lookup_url_kwarg - The URL keyword argument that should be used for object lookup.
HyperlinkedRelatedField may be used to represent the target of the relationship using a hyperlink.

When instantiating a HyperlinkedModelSerializer you must include the current request in the serializer context, for example: serializer = AccountSerializer ( queryset , context ={ 'request' : request }) Doing so will ensure that the hyperlinks can include an appropriate hostname, so that the resulting representation uses fully qualified URLs, such as: http : //api.example.com/accounts/1/ Rather than relative URLs, such as: /accounts/ 1 / If you do want to use relative URLs, you should explicitly pass {'request': None} in the serializer context.
llm_response:
To resolve hyperlinks when using a custom `lookup_field`, you must ensure that the `lookup_field` defined in your serializer matches the lookup field expected by your URL configuration.

You can configure this in one of two ways:

*   **Using `extra_kwargs`:** Define the `lookup_field` within the `extra_kwargs` dictionary in your serializer's `Meta` class:
    ```python
    class MySerializer(serializers.HyperlinkedModelSerializer):
        class Meta:
            model = MyModel
            fields = ['url', ...]
            extra_kwargs = {'url': {'lookup_field': 'uuid'}}
    ```
*   **Explicitly defining the field:** Define the `url` field explicitly on the serializer class using `HyperlinkedIdentityField` (or `HyperlinkedRelatedField` for relationships) and provide the `lookup_field` argument:
    ```python
    class MySerializer(serializers.HyperlinkedModelSerializer):
        url = serializers.HyperlinkedIdentityField(view_name='mymodel-detail', lookup_field='uuid')
        class Meta:
            model = MyModel
            fields = ['url', ...]
    ```

The documentation recommends printing the `repr` of your `HyperlinkedModelSerializer` instance to inspect exactly which view names and lookup fields the relationships are expected to map to, as matching these with your URL configuration can be "fiddly."

user_input: Our album list endpoint went from 40ms to about four seconds after I changed the tracks field to render the full nested track objects instead of just their ids. Someone told me to add select_related('tracks') to the queryset and the ORM threw an error at me instead. Why doesn't the framework deal with this itself, and how do I tell which optimisation goes with which field?
reference: The framework deliberately doesn't optimise the queryset for you — it makes no attempt to infer select_related / prefetch_related from your serializer, because that would be too much magic. Any field that spans an ORM relation, whether it's a declared relational field or a plain field reaching across a relation via `source`, can cost an extra query per object, and with many=True over a large queryset that becomes the N+1 you're seeing. Fixing it is your job, and which tool applies is decided by the relation, not by the serializer: select_related resolves forward single-valued relations (ForeignKey, OneToOne) with a SQL join, while a reverse or multi-valued relation like `tracks` cannot be joined that way and has to use prefetch_related — which is exactly why select_related('tracks') errored. Pass the optimised queryset to the serializer (Album.objects.prefetch_related('tracks')) and the extra hits disappear.
reference_contexts: REST Framework does not attempt to automatically optimize querysets passed to serializers in terms of select_related and prefetch_related since it would be too much magic. A serializer with a field spanning an ORM relation through its source attribute could require an additional database hit to fetch related objects from the database. It is the programmer's responsibility to optimize queries to avoid additional database hits which could occur while using a serializer.
If AlbumSerializer is used to serialize a fairly large queryset with many=True then it could be a serious performance problem.
qs = Album.objects.prefetch_related('tracks') # No additional database hits required print(AlbumSerializer(qs, many=True).data)
llm_response:
The framework does not automatically optimize querysets because it would be "too much magic" [4]. It is the programmer's responsibility to optimize queries to avoid the N+1 query pattern that occurs when serializers access related objects individually for each item [1, 4].

To determine which optimization to use, you must identify the type of relationship [1]:

*   **`select_related()`**: Use this for `ForeignKey` and `OneToOneField` relationships to fetch related objects in the same database query [1].
*   **`prefetch_related()`**: Use this for reverse and many-to-many relationships to efficiently load collections of related objects [1].

Because `tracks` is a collection (many-to-many or reverse relationship), you must use `prefetch_related('tracks')` instead of `select_related('tracks')` to resolve your performance issue [1, 5].

reference: For new users, catch the user post_save signal and Token.objects.create(user=instance) when created; for existing users, loop User.objects.all() and Token.objects.get_or_create(user=user).

llm_response:
To automatically generate an auth token for every user at account creation, use the `post_save` signal. Place the following code in an installed `models.py` module or another location imported by Django on startup:

```python
from django.conf import settings
from django.db.models.signals import post_save
from django.dispatch import receiver
from rest_framework.authtoken.models import Token

@receiver(post_save, sender=settings.AUTH_USER_MODEL)
def create_auth_token(sender, instance=None, created=False, **kwargs):
    if created:
        Token.objects.create(user=instance)
```

To backfill tokens for existing users, use the following loop:

```python
from django.contrib.auth.models import User
from rest_framework.authtoken.models import Token

for user in User.objects.all():
    Token.objects.get_or_create(user=user)
```
